opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more important caveats people should keep in mind when they look at benchmark numbers. SWE-bench grades a solution by whether it passes the repository's tests. But "passes the tests" and "a maintainer would actually merge this" are quite different bars. When we had people with real maintainer-level familiarity look at AI-generated patches that passed, a substantial fraction wouldn't have been accepted as-is. The reasons were things like poor code quality, not following the project's conventions, missing documentation or tests, changes that technically fix the symptom but in a hacky or brittle way, or patches that touch things they shouldn't.

How I interpret it is roughly this. The benchmark score is real signal. These models are genuinely getting much better at localizing bugs and producing working fixes, and that trend matters. But the headline number overstates how much autonomous, real-world value you'd get if you dropped the model into an actual project with no human cleanup. There's a gap between "algorithmically scorable success" and "holistically good work," and that gap is exactly the kind of messy, hard-to-specify stuff that real jobs are full of.

From a forecasting and risk perspective, that's important in both directions. You don't want to dismiss the capability gains. The rate of improvement is fast, and some of the mergeability gap is probably closable with better scaffolding, more context about project norms, or just the next model generation. But you also don't want to read a benchmark saturating as "this task is solved." When we try to translate benchmark performance into something like "what fraction of a human engineer's work could this do," we should probably apply some discount for this sort of thing. We should also measure it directly where we can, rather than assuming test-passing is a good proxy.

More broadly, I think it's a reminder that a lot of our measurement leans toward tasks that are easy to score automatically, and those may systematically flatter the models relative to the open-ended, judgment-heavy parts of real work. So part of the research agenda is figuring out how big that discount is, and whether it's shrinking over time as fast as the raw scores are rising.

r001.rationale: The response says a substantial fraction of test-passing patches would not be accepted as-is, but gives no roughly half rate or comparison with previously merged human solutions.

r002.rationale: It says the mergeability gap may be closable and model capabilities are improving, but does not state that maintainer-assessed mergeability is increasing over time.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe a rise over time in mergeability among AI solutions that pass SWE-bench tests.

r004.rationale: It treats test-passing performance as real signal, but does not suggest that progress on automatically checkable performance is driving improved maintainer-assessed mergeability.

fable-5.1.text:
So, when we looked at the maintainer mergeability results, the thing that jumped out to me is just how big the gap is between "passes the tests" and "a maintainer would actually merge this." A lot of the solutions that get counted as successes on SWE-bench are, in the words of the people who actually own these repos, not something they'd accept. They're brittle, or they special-case the failing test, or they ignore conventions in the codebase, or they fix the symptom without touching the underlying cause.

And I think that's really informative about what the benchmark is and isn't measuring. SWE-bench measures "can you make the hidden tests go green," and that's a real skill, but it's a pretty narrow proxy for "can you do the job of a software engineer." The job includes understanding what the maintainers want, writing something that fits into the existing design, and not creating a maintenance burden for the next person. Those things are exactly where we see the models falling short, and they're also exactly the things a test suite can't easily check.

So there are two ways I'd interpret it. The pessimistic read is that headline SWE-bench numbers are overstating real-world capability, maybe by a lot, and we should be cautious about saying "models can do X percent of software engineering tasks." The more nuanced read is that it's not that the models can't do these things, it's that the incentive the benchmark creates doesn't reward them. If you reward passing tests, you get test-passing. When we've looked at this kind of thing more generally, models are very sensitive to what you're actually scoring, so to some extent you'd expect this.

From our perspective at METR, the thing we care about is whether these evaluations are telling us something true about autonomous capability in the world. If the metric diverges from what humans would actually accept, that's a problem for anyone trying to use these numbers for forecasting or for making decisions about deployment. So I'd treat mergeability as a correction factor on top of pass rates, and I'd encourage people to look at both. It also argues for evaluations that involve human judgment or longer-horizon outcomes, even though those are more expensive and noisier to run.

The last thing I'd say is, this is a moving target. Some of these failure modes, like not matching codebase style, are the sort of thing that labs can and will train out fairly quickly once they're measured. Others, like genuinely understanding a maintainer's intent from an ambiguous issue, might be harder. So I wouldn't take the current gap as a fixed fact about what models can do. I'd take it as a reminder that we should be measuring what we actually care about, and being honest about where our proxies fall short.

r001.rationale: It says many test-passing solutions would not be accepted by maintainers, but gives no roughly half-rate comparison with previously merged human reference solutions.

r002.rationale: It describes current shortcomings and says some failure modes may be trained out, but does not suggest that maintainer-assessed mergeability is increasing over time.

r003.rationale: It does not describe a time trend in mergeability among AI solutions that pass the tests.

r004.rationale: It discusses benchmark incentives and future training, but does not suggest that improving automatically checkable SWE-bench performance is driving better mergeability.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between passing the tests and producing a patch that a maintainer would actually want to merge. Those are related, but they’re not the same thing. A patch can pass the tests and still miss part of the intended behavior, be unnecessarily complicated, or fit poorly with the rest of the codebase.

So I’d interpret maintainer mergeability as an additional check on what SWE-bench performance means in practice. If maintainers reject a substantial fraction of solutions that pass, that limits the claim that those issues have really been solved. But I wouldn’t conclude that the patches are therefore useless: something that needs a small revision might still save a developer time.

What I’d really want to understand is why they aren’t mergeable and how much human work remains. Is it a straightforward cleanup, or does someone have to identify a subtle flaw and rethink the solution? That distinction matters a lot for translating benchmark scores into useful automation.

r001.rationale: It discusses maintainer rejection of test-passing patches only hypothetically and gives no comparison with human reference solutions or approximate half-rate.

r002.rationale: It does not say maintainer-assessed mergeability is increasing over time.

r003.rationale: It does not describe a time trend in mergeability among test-passing AI solutions.

r004.rationale: It does not connect improvements in automatically checkable benchmark performance to improving maintainer-assessed mergeability.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d interpret them as a useful check on what passing SWE-bench actually means. Getting a patch to pass the tests is evidence that it solves some version of the problem, but it doesn’t necessarily mean a maintainer would want to merge it. They might care about whether it fits the codebase, whether it introduces unnecessary complexity, or whether it handles cases the tests don’t cover.

But I’d also distinguish “I wouldn’t merge this as submitted” from “this isn’t useful.” Human contributions often need review and revision too. The interesting question is how much work remains for the maintainer, and whether the system can respond to feedback and get the patch into a mergeable state. So I’d treat those results as evidence about the gap between benchmark success and useful software engineering, rather than as a single verdict on the systems’ capabilities.

r001.rationale: It says passing tests does not guarantee maintainers would merge a patch, but gives no comparison with human reference solutions or rate of about half.

r002.rationale: It does not say maintainer-assessed mergeability is increasing over time.

r003.rationale: It does not describe a time trend in mergeability among AI solutions that pass the tests.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest that improvements in automatically checkable benchmark performance are driving mergeability improvements.
